idiom_name: async/await I/O layer plus a bounded Channel<T> drained by Task.Run workers
implementation_notes: The asynchronous layer is ordinary async/await over sockets or HTTP, where the runtime's I/O completion machinery demultiplexes instead of a thread; the queueing layer is a bounded Channel<T> and the synchronous layer is a small set of long-running Task workers started with Task.Run that drain it with await foreach over ReadAllAsync(). BlockingCollection<T> remains the classic alternative where a strictly blocking consumer loop is wanted. Never block the I/O layer (no .Result, no .Wait(), no lock held across an await): a blocked thread-pool thread is the thing this split exists to avoid.
pitfalls: Blocking a worker with .Result or .Wait() on the async I/O layer converts concurrency into thread-pool starvation.
A bounded channel must be given a FullMode: the default Wait parks producers forever and looks like a hang unless cancellation and timeouts are handled.
Task.Run workers are thread-pool threads; a worker that blocks for the duration of a long job needs TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning or a dedicated thread.

variants.name: BlockingCollection<T> with dedicated consumer threads
variants.idiom_name: BlockingCollection<T> over a ConcurrentQueue with a dedicated consumer thread per worker
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-Channels .NET idiom: a bounded BlockingCollection<T> is the queueing layer, producers add from the asynchronous callbacks (APM or async/await) and a fixed set of dedicated threads blocks in a foreach over GetConsumingEnumerable(). Choose it when targeting .NET Framework or when a purely blocking consumer loop matches existing service code; it costs one OS thread per consumer and offers no async read API.
pitfalls: Mixing Take() with async code deadlocks the thread pool under load; the consumer must stay purely blocking, or use the Channel variant instead.
GetConsumingEnumerable() never returns until CompleteAdding() is called during shutdown, otherwise workers park forever.
